opus-5.5.text:
Thanks for having me. It's a question I think about almost every day.

The short answer is that we're placing a big bet on end-to-end, but we're doing it with our eyes open. For a long time robotics was built as a pipeline: perception, then state estimation, then planning, then control. Each module had its own team, its own metrics, its own failure modes. It worked in structured settings like factories, but every time we moved into the messy real world the errors piled up at the boundaries between modules. A perception system can be 99% accurate and the robot still drops the cup, because the planner never knew what the perception system was uncertain about.

What changed in the last few years is that large models showed us a different path. If you train one model that goes from pixels and language directly to actions, it can learn representations that serve the task, not a human-designed interface between modules. And when you build that on a vision-language backbone, you get something we never had before: common sense. The robot already understands what a banana is, what "put it near the blue thing" means, roughly how objects behave, before it has seen a single robot demonstration.

So how do we invest? I'd describe it in three layers.

First, the model itself. We want one unified model that handles reasoning and acting together, rather than a high-level brain that hands off to a separate low-level controller. In practice we still have some hierarchy inside, a slower part that thinks and a faster part that acts, but it's trained jointly and it's one system. Embodied reasoning, things like spatial understanding, predicting trajectories, and understanding affordances, is a capability we deliberately push, because that's where general vision-language models are still weak.

Second, and honestly the harder part, is data. Language models had the internet. Robotics has no internet of actions. So a large share of our effort goes into data: teleoperation at scale, getting data across many different robot embodiments so the model learns something more general than one arm's quirks, using simulation where it helps, and increasingly learning from human videos. Cross-embodiment transfer is one of the most encouraging things we've seen. Data from one robot genuinely helps another.

Third is evaluation. This is underrated. When your model is end-to-end, you lose the ability to unit test each module, so you need very good ways to measure generalization: new objects, new scenes, new instructions. Real-world evaluation is slow and expensive, so we invest a lot in making it more systematic, and in exploring whether learned world models or simulation can serve as proxies.

I'll be honest about the trade-offs. End-to-end models are data hungry, harder to interpret, and safety is a real concern when you can't easily point to the line of code that made a decision. So we keep some guardrails outside the model, especially for low-level safety, and we take the semantic side of safety seriously too, making sure the robot understands when an instruction shouldn't be carried out.

But if you ask me where the long-term value is, I'm fairly convinced it's the unified approach. Every time we've scaled data and model size together, capability has gone up in ways the modular systems never achieved. The question isn't really whether end-to-end will win. It's how fast we can solve the data problem to get there.

r001.rationale: The response describes a broad, long-term bet on end-to-end models and mentions internal hierarchy and safety guardrails, but it does not identify short-term proof-of-concept work as an exception.

fable-5.1.text:
I'd put it this way: we're not investing in a model architecture, we're investing in a bet about where the bottleneck in AI shifts next.

For the past few years, the stack has been modular. You had a language model, a separate vision encoder, a speech recognition front end, a text-to-speech module on the back, maybe a planner or a tool router in the middle. Each piece could be best-in-class, and you glued them together. That worked, but every seam leaks. You lose information at each handoff, latency compounds, and the system can't learn from its own end-to-end mistakes because the error never flows back through the whole pipeline.

End-to-end unified models say: stop gluing. Train one model that takes in text, image, audio, video, action, and produces any of those back, with a single objective. The appeal is obvious. The question for us as investors is whether that's a research direction or a company.

So we look at three things.

First, who actually has the data and compute to make unification pay off? Unified models are expensive to train and the gains show up late in the scaling curve. A startup that says "we're building the unified model" without a credible path to tens of thousands of GPUs and proprietary multimodal data is, frankly, writing a paper, not a business. We've mostly stayed away from that layer in China unless there's a strategic backer with real infrastructure.

Second, where does unification create a product that the modular approach simply can't deliver? That's where we've been more active. Real-time voice agents are one example. If you chain ASR, LLM, and TTS, you're at a second or two of latency and you lose tone, interruption, emotion. A native speech-in, speech-out model changes the experience qualitatively. Embodied AI is another. Robots need perception and action in one loop, and the modular stack is just too slow and too brittle. In both cases the unified model isn't a nicety, it's the enabler.

Third, we think about the application layer differently now. Our view is that unified foundation models will become a utility, and the moat will come from vertical data, distribution, and workflow integration. So we're backing teams that are building on top of these models but accumulating something the model provider can't easily replicate, whether that's a physical fleet, a regulated dataset, or a deep customer relationship.

One honest caveat. Unified doesn't always mean better. For a lot of enterprise use cases, a smaller specialized model is cheaper and more controllable, and the customer doesn't care that it's elegant. So we're trying not to be ideological. We fund where the unification unlocks a real step change, and we're skeptical where it's just a cleaner architecture diagram.

r001.rationale: The response discusses investment in unified end-to-end models and when they may be useful, but does not identify short-term proof-of-concept work as an exception to Jie Tan’s modeling approach.

astra-6.text:
I’d approach it as a long-term research investment, with clear milestones along the way. The appeal of an end-to-end unified model is that different capabilities can improve together. But putting everything into one model doesn’t automatically make the system better.

The key question is whether unification produces measurable gains: better generalization, more efficient learning, and more reliable performance on real tasks. I’d invest in the model alongside the data and evaluation infrastructure needed to answer that question.

I’d also keep strong modular baselines. If the unified approach outperforms them, that gives us a reason to scale the investment. Where it struggles, we need to understand whether the limitation is data, training, or the architecture itself. So the direction is ambitious, but the investment should follow evidence.

r001.rationale: The candidate describes a long-term research investment with milestones, but does not identify short-term proof-of-concept work as an exception to an otherwise end-to-end approach.

sol-6.1.text:
I’d approach it by separating the long-term direction from the investment decision today. End-to-end unified models are a compelling direction, but that alone doesn’t tell you which team or product will create lasting value.

I’d look at three things: whether the team can keep improving the model, whether it has access to useful data and a strong feedback loop, and whether those improvements translate into something customers will pay for. You also have to account for inference costs and reliability. A model can be impressive in a demonstration and still be difficult to build a business around.

So I’d invest in stages, with clear technical and commercial milestones. The key question is whether greater unification produces a measurable advantage in a real application.

r001.rationale: The response discusses staged investment and technical and commercial milestones, but does not identify short-term proof-of-concept work as an exception to an otherwise end-to-end modeling approach.
